key.why: The second function takes bob before alice, the opposite of the first. Either of those two lines is the one to change.

explanation:
## Line 9 — `bob_pays_alice` takes the locks in the opposite order

Every line here is correct in isolation. The bug is a **relationship between two functions**, which is why it survives review of either one.

```
alice_pays_bob:   alice.m  then  bob.m
bob_pays_alice:   bob.m    then  alice.m
```

Interleave two threads:

| | Thread 1 (`alice_pays_bob`) | Thread 2 (`bob_pays_alice`) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | takes `alice.m` | |
| 2 | | takes `bob.m` |
| 3 | waits for `bob.m` | |
| 4 | | waits for `alice.m` |

Each holds what the other needs, and neither will ever let go, because `lock_guard` releases only at the end of the scope and neither thread will reach it. Both threads sleep forever. No CPU is used, no error is reported, nothing is logged. The process simply stops doing that kind of work.

## Why it took weeks to show up

The window in which it can happen is the handful of instructions between thread 1 taking the first lock and the second. Both threads have to be inside their respective windows at the same moment. Under light load that is vanishingly unlikely; under heavy load with many threads it becomes a matter of time.

This is the characteristic signature of a lock-order bug: **it does not reproduce, and then one day in production it does.** It is also why you cannot test your way to confidence here and have to reason about the order instead.

## The fix: one global order, written down

Pick an order for every lock in the program and never deviate. Here, lock in address order, which is arbitrary but consistent and needs no extra bookkeeping:

```cpp
void transfer(Account& from, Account& to, long amount) {
    Account* first  = &from < &to ? &from : &to;
    Account* second = &from < &to ? &to   : &from;

    std::lock_guard<std::mutex> l1(first->m);
    std::lock_guard<std::mutex> l2(second->m);

    from.balance -= amount;
    to.balance   += amount;
}
```

Now no two threads can disagree about the order, so the cycle cannot form.

## Better: let the library do it

C++ has this built in, and it is what you should reach for:

```cpp
void transfer(Account& from, Account& to, long amount) {
    std::scoped_lock lock(from.m, to.m);   // both, or neither
    from.balance -= amount;
    to.balance   += amount;
}
```

`std::scoped_lock` (and `std::lock` before it) takes all the mutexes with a deadlock-avoidance algorithm: it tries, and on failure releases everything it holds and retries. The order you pass them in does not matter. One line, no ordering convention to remember, no address comparison.

This is the general shape of the lesson: **nested lock acquisition is the thing to avoid**, and when you cannot avoid it, acquire all at once rather than one at a time.

## The four conditions, and which one you break

A deadlock needs all four of mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, and circular wait. You cannot drop mutual exclusion — that is the point of the lock. In practice you break **circular wait** with a global order, which is the `scoped_lock` fix, or you break **hold-and-wait** with `try_lock` and a back-off.

## Finding them

- **ThreadSanitizer** (`-fsanitize=thread`) detects lock-order inversions *the first time it sees both orders*, without needing the deadlock to actually occur. That is the single most valuable thing about it, and it would have caught this on the first test run.
- `gdb -p <pid>` then `thread apply all bt` on a hung process shows you two stacks both sitting in `__lll_lock_wait`, holding the answer.
- Writing the lock order into a comment at the top of the file sounds quaint and works.
